summary: Chang She and Noah Shpak present on training dataset development for LLMs, combining Character AI's practical data platform experience with LanceDB's storage infrastructure. Noah explains that pre-training focuses on broad domains and quantity (books vs. chat data, token counts), while post-training requires granular, task-specific understanding (difficulty levels, problem structure). Character AI's hierarchy of needs starts with clean data and evaluations, then emphasizes dataset management for mixtures with rich analytics—token counts, code classification beyond language into difficulty and structure. Key techniques include data-efficient learning, diversity measurement, dataset selection via retrieval/clustering to match distributions, quality scoring with classifiers or prompting, synthetic data generation for rapid exploration, and human labeling for improving classifiers and rewriting problematic data. Noah highlights that their materialization service separates data materialization from training jobs, reducing errors. A YAML interface with embedded SQL lets researchers define datasets declaratively. LanceDB's fast random access enables shuffling row references rather than rows themselves, saving iteration time. Chang frames the core infrastructure problem: distributed training needs fast scans (filtering), fast random access (shuffling), and efficient large blob streaming—existing formats satisfy at most two of three, constituting a 'CAP theorem for AI data.' Scale exacerbates this: tabular rows average ~50 bytes, embeddings add 20-25x, images another 20x, and generative AI produces data at thousands of tokens per second, with small teams managing tens of terabytes to petabytes. Lance format addresses this as a columnar format like Parquet but optimized for AI, supporting fast scans, fast lookups (unlike Parquet), inline blob storage without Parquet's row group limitation, zero-copy schema evolution, time travel for instant rollback, and indexing extensions. Lance adds indexing for embeddings (billion-scale vector search off S3), scalar indices for fast metadata filtering, and full-text search indices—potentially eliminating separate Elasticsearch clusters. This enables a single table serving many workloads: SQL via DuckDB/Trino/Spark, training via PyTorch, and vector similarity search. LanceDB provides distributed vector search at billion scale with order-of-magnitude less infrastructure than other vector databases. Chang highlights that multimodality spans data (features, audio, images, vectors), workloads (SQL, vector search, full-text search, filtering), and use cases (production RAG/search/personalization, training, data lake analysis). Noah closes by emphasizing speed as their core strategy, noting existing tools slow down under new multimodal demands.

sections.title: Speaker introductions
sections.summary: Chang She introduces himself as CEO/co-founder of LanceDB, with two decades in data tools including co-authoring pandas. Noah introduces his role leading the AI data platform at Character AI, focusing on research acceleration, data mining, prompting tools, and retrieval systems.

sections.title: Pre-training vs post-training data considerations
sections.summary: Noah contrasts pre-training (wider domain coverage, quantity concerns like model size and token counts) with post-training (granular task-specific understanding like difficulty levels). He mentions active research areas: data-efficient learning, sampling metrics, and diversity measurement.

sections.title: Hierarchy of needs and data improvement techniques
sections.summary: Noah presents a hierarchy starting with clean data and evaluations, then dataset management with rich analytics for mixtures (token counts, code classification into difficulty and structure). Key techniques include dataset selection via retrieval/clustering to match distributions, quality scoring with classifiers or prompting, synthetic data for rapid exploration, and human labeling for improving classifiers and rewriting problematic data.

sections.title: Materialization service and data loading with Lance
sections.summary: Noah shows a YAML interface with embedded SQL for declarative dataset materialization, separating data materialization from training jobs to reduce errors. Lance's fast random access enables shuffling row references instead of rows themselves, saving iteration time. The goal is maximizing GPU utilization.

sections.title: CAP theorem for AI data and scale challenges
sections.summary: Chang introduces the 'CAP theorem for AI data': distributed training requires fast scans (filtering), fast random access (shuffling), and large blob streaming—existing formats satisfy at most two. Scale compounds this: tabular rows ~50 bytes, embeddings 20-25x larger, images another 20x, with small teams managing terabytes to petabytes.

sections.title: Lance format features
sections.summary: Chang details Lance format: columnar like Parquet but AI-optimized, supporting fast scans and fast lookups (unlike Parquet), inline blob storage without row group limitations, zero-copy schema evolution, time travel for instant rollback, and indexing extensions enabling both identifying and quickly fetching needed rows.

sections.title: Lance indexing extensions and LanceDB for multimodal AI
sections.summary: Chang describes Lance's indexing extensions: billion-scale vector search off S3, scalar indices for fast metadata filtering, and full-text search indices—potentially eliminating separate Elasticsearch. A single Lance table serves many workloads: SQL via DuckDB/Trino/Spark, training via PyTorch, and vector similarity search. LanceDB provides distributed vector search with order-of-magnitude less infrastructure than competitors. Multimodality spans three dimensions: data types (features, audio, images, vectors), workloads (SQL, vector search, full-text search, filtering), and use cases (production RAG/search/personalization, training, data lake analysis). Noah closes emphasizing speed as their core strategy, noting existing tools slow down under new multimodal demands.
